subject: Air-gapped egress policy design scenarios
messages:
From: Markus Klein <markus_klein@redwood.ai>
To: Elaine Roberts <elaine@clearwaterhealth.com>, Nick Sullivan <nsullivan@corp-ops.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 14 Oct 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Design options for air-gapped private endpoint egress

Elaine / Nick —

Thanks for the walkthrough earlier. As we discussed, Clearwater's on-prem deployment needs a strict "no direct internet" posture for the model runtime control plane. I sketched three pragmatic options we commonly use for customers in regulated environments; wanted to capture them here and get your constraints back so we can pick the right path. Attached: egress-diagram-v2.png (diagram), control-plane-egress-checklist.xlsx (asks we need).

High-level options (tradeoffs in short):
1) Managed Relay (preferred where possible)
   - Customer establishes a TLS+client-cert authenticated outbound tunnel (TLS mutual auth) from a bastion in their network to a Redwood-managed relay in a customer region.
   - Only outbound connections allowed from customer to relay; relay performs egress to Redwood control plane.
   - Firewall needs: allow outbound to relay IPs/ports only (443/TCP); DNS FQDNs locked; no inbound required.
   - Pros: minimal attack surface, simple IP allowlist on firewall, preserves airgap characteristics since no inbound from internet.

2) Partner Proxy/NAT with Strict Allowlist
   - Customer uses an internal egress proxy/NAT that allows traffic only to specific Redwood IP ranges and FQDNs.
   - Requires static egress IPs (or small pool) and strong TLS verification (SNI and cert pinning recommended).
   - Firewall: permit outbound to listed IPs and to TLS port 443; block other internet destinations.
   - Pros: works with existing proxy infra; less infra change.

3) Offline Batch Exchange (airgap-preserving fallback)
   - No persistent outbound egress. Customer and Redwood exchange tokens/requests via scheduled, signed bundles (SFTP or removable media workflow) — good for extreme offline requirements.
   - Firewall: no outbound to internet needed for runtime, only administrative transfer channels as agreed.
   - Pros: highest isolation, but higher latency and operational overhead.

Minimum allowlist & control-plane requirements we need from your side to evaluate (short):
- Whether outbound to a small set of static IPs (or short-lived delegated IPs) is acceptable.
- If you have a corporate egress proxy, does it support mTLS client certs and SNI preservation?
- Any mandated ports/protocol forbiddances (e.g., no DNS over UDP allowed, only DNS over TLS)?
- Which VLANs/subnets will host the runtime (CIDR + responsible owner)?
- Compliance evidence timeline (SOC2/audit) for where logs will be retained.

Next steps: if you can confirm the above constraints, we will produce a minimal IP/FQDN allowlist + firewall ACL snippets and a proposed mutual-auth TLS config for the relay option.

Thanks —
Markus Klein
Sr. Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
markus_klein@redwood.ai

Attachments: egress-diagram-v2.png (diagram, 1.2MB stub), control-plane-egress-checklist.xlsx (questionnaire stub)

From: Elaine Roberts <elaine@clearwaterhealth.com>
To: Markus Klein <markus_klein@redwood.ai>
Cc: Nick Sullivan <nsullivan@corp-ops.com>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 15 Oct 2026 10:05:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Design options for air-gapped private endpoint egress

Markus —

Thanks for the clear options. Quick context on our side: Clearwater's clinical analytics cluster is completely zero-inbound except for internal management. We cannot accept arbitrary outbound to the public internet. Our preferred pattern is an egress proxy that we control (corporate proxy) that validates client certs and allows only specific destinations.

Constraints:
- No direct inbound allowed at any time.
- Outbound only via our proxy at 10.10.200.5 (proxy performs TLS termination for outbound).
- We can allow a /28 of static outbound NAT IPs if needed but prefer to map at FQDN level.
- DNS policy: DNS over TLS is required; UDP DNS is denied.
- We will require mTLS on any externally facing tunnel and proof of chain-of-custody for keys.

Can you produce the exact IPs/FQDNs Redwood needs and an example mTLS config so we can validate against our proxy? Also, if you have an architecture that avoids opening any additional ports beyond 443 outbound from our side, that's preferred.

—Elaine
Elaine Roberts
Head of Platform Operations, Clearwater Health
elaine@clearwaterhealth.com

From: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>
To: Elaine Roberts <elaine@clearwaterhealth.com>, Markus Klein <markus_klein@redwood.ai>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 19 Oct 2026 08:22:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Design options for air-gapped private endpoint egress

Elaine —

Appreciate the constraints. Below is a practical deliverable we can provide once you confirm which option you want to pursue.

If you pick Managed Relay (recommended):
- We will publish a small set of region-scoped relay IPs (two HA addresses per region) and relay FQDNs.
- Required customer firewall rules: allow outbound TCP/443 to relay IPs; allow DNS over TLS to resolve relay FQDNs (we can provide DNS entries).
- Mutual TLS: Redwood will accept client certs you present; we will provide CSR/CA guidance.
- Logging/audit: Relay will forward structured audit logs to your SIEM via an agreed collector (we can push to your SFTP or to a configured syslog endpoint).

If you pick Partner Proxy/NAT:
- We'll supply exact FQDNs and a small pool of static egress IPs for redirection; we recommend SNI-based allowlisting and cert pinning.

If you pick Offline Batch:
- We'll provide signed bundle format docs and SFTP keys for scheduled exchange.

Checklist we need from you to finalize the ACL snippets (I've attached a short template as control-plane-egress-checklist.xlsx):
- Confirm outbound NAT behavior (static IPs vs ephemeral)
- Which subnets will be used for runtime and for management
- Who owns the proxy (team contact + escalation)
- Whether you require mTLS client cert rotation cadence (we recommend 90 days)

Action: Markus / Ben — can you draft the relay IPs and the minimum firewall ACL snippets (iptables / Palo Alto / AWS NACL examples) and upload to the Confluence page linked below? Elaine — once we have that, we can schedule a firewall rules verification call with your network team.

Laura Bennett
Director, Platform Solutions, Redwood Inference
laura_bennett@redwood.ai

Attachments: control-plane-egress-checklist.xlsx
Confluence draft: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/PRIVATE/Airgap-Egress-Patterns

From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
To: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>, Markus Klein <markus_klein@redwood.ai>, Elaine Roberts <elaine@clearwaterhealth.com>
Date: Wed, 21 Oct 2026 09:34:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Design options for air-gapped private endpoint egress

Laura / Markus / Elaine —

Quick technical note and preliminary IP set. We validated feasibility for the Managed Relay pattern against our infra team. If Clearwater can egress to the following addresses we can keep traffic strictly over 443 and enforce mTLS:
- 52.203.167.210 (relay-us-west-2-01.redwood-inference.net)
- 52.203.167.211 (relay-us-west-2-02.redwood-inference.net)
- 54.210.34.18 (relay-us-east-1-01.redwood-inference.net)

Firewall snippets (example):
- Palo Alto: rule permit outbound tcp 443 source <runtime-subnet> dest 52.203.167.210/32,52.203.167.211/32 service application-tls; deny internet-other after rule.
- iptables (example): iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp -d 52.203.167.210 --dport 443 -j ACCEPT; iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp -d 52.203.167.211 --dport 443 -j ACCEPT; iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j DROP

Notes:
- We will support DNS over TLS if your proxy can resolve the relay FQDNs; otherwise we can provide static /32 entries.
- For mTLS, Redwood will present a server cert chain; you will present the client cert. We will provide a sample nginx-style mTLS config and CSR flow.

Uploaded my draft ACL examples and an IP list to the Confluence page. Also added a short fallback plan: if the proxy cannot perform cert passthrough, we can use the static IPs and lock by IP + cert pinning on application layer.

Ben Carter
Security Solutions, Redwood Inference
ben_carter@redwood.ai

Attachment: ip-list-for-inbound.xlsx (stub)
